prove.theorem:
Definitions: a box is a closed axis-parallel box with positive side lengths. It is strict if its three side lengths are pairwise distinct. A tiling is a finite family of boxes whose union is the big box and whose interiors are pairwise disjoint. Following the A386884 name and comment, and A386903 (of which it is column 4), A386884(n) (offset 1) is the number of SETS of four pairwise noncongruent strict shapes (x,y,z), with positive integer sides, such that [0,n]^3 can be tiled by four boxes with exactly those shapes.

Theorem: for every n >= 1, A386884(n) = (n-4)*T(ceil((n-4)/2)) with T(j) = j(j+1)/2. Equivalently, with m = floor((n-1)/2), A386884(n) = C(m,2) + m(m-1)(m-2) + [n even]*C(m,2), which is m(m-1)(2m-3)/2 for n = 2m+1 and m(m-1)^2 for n = 2m+2.

Consequences:
- a(1..4) = 0, and A386884(n) = A178312(n-4) for all n >= 4.
- The g.f. is x^5(1+x+4x^2)/((1+x)^3(1-x)^4).
- a(n) = (n-4)(2(n-4)(n-1) - (2n-5)(-1)^n + 3)/16.
- The order-7 recurrence with signature (1,3,-3,-3,3,1,-1) holds for n >= 8.

Supporting results also proved:
(1) Guillotine lemma: every tiling of a box by 2 <= k <= 4 boxes has a guillotine plane. This is false for k = 5.
(2) Structure: every tiling of the n-cube by 4 strict integer-sided boxes is two slabs n x n x t and n x n x (n-t), each cut once across. Its shapes are {s,t,n}, {n-s,t,n}, {s',n-t,n}, {n-s',n-t,n} with 1 <= t <= n-1 and s, s' in [1,n-1] \ {t, n-t}. Every such parameter triple gives a tiling.
(3) Appendix: any tiling of a box by possibly rotated boxes has all tiles axis-parallel. With integer sides, all positions are integers.
prove.proof_summary:
Guillotine lemma. Each corner of the box lies in exactly one tile. A tile holding 3 or more corners, or 2 corners not on a common edge, is full in two directions, and then one of its faces is a guillotine plane. Otherwise there are 8 corners, at most 4 tiles and at most 2 corners per tile, so each tile holds exactly the two endpoints of an edge of B. This is the only place where k <= 4 is used; in the pinwheel a tile holds no corner. These edges form a perfect matching of the cube graph, and a parity count shows it has one of two types:
- All four edges parallel: the edge segments of B force a1+a2 = L1, a3+a4 = L1, b1+b4 = L2 and b2+b3 = L2. Volume additivity then gives (a1-a4)(b1-b2) = 0, which yields a guillotine plane.
- Two parallel edges on one face and two perpendicular edges on the opposite face: the vertical edge segments force all four heights to meet at one level h, and z = h is a guillotine plane.

Structure. Cut the cube along a guillotine plane into two slabs n x n x t and n x n x (n-t). Neither slab is strict, so each holds exactly 2 tiles. Applying the lemma with k = 2, each slab is cut once, perpendicular to an n-direction. This gives the shape sets Sigma(t,s,s'), and conversely every valid triple is realised.

Counting. Encode shape {x,y,n} as the edge {x,y} on [n-1] and use the involution x -> n-x. The sets of shapes split into three types, each counted exactly:
- the 4-cycles O1 x O2: C(m,2);
- two disjoint cherries {t}xO1 u {n-t}xO2: m(m-1)(m-2);
- for n even, stars {n/2}x(O1 u O2): C(m,2).
The three types have 4, 6 and 5 vertices, so their images are disjoint. Simplifying the sum gives (n-4)T(ceil((n-4)/2)).

verify.independent_computation:
I wrote my own code in /tmp/claude-0/deep/cuboids/verify1/ and did not reuse the colleague's code. tile.c enumerates every tiling of a P x Q x R integer grid by exactly K boxes. Boxes 1..K-1 are placed at the first empty cell (z,y,x order) with free-space early breaks. The last box must equal [first free cell, last free cell + 1], checked by volume and disjointness. From each tiling it takes the set of sorted shapes, keeps those with 4 pairwise-distinct shapes (strict or not), and deduplicates. It does not use the guillotine lemma or the structure theorem; it relies only on integer positions, which I checked as Lemma B.

(1) Direct counts of the n-cube by this method:
- Strict, n = 1..13: 0,0,0,0,1,2,9,12,30,36,70,80,135, matching A386884 and the formula.
- Non-strict, n = 1..8: 0,0,4,12,47,85,183,266, matching A384311. This confirms the "set of pairwise noncongruent shapes" reading. A multiset reading would give a(4) >= 1, since {1,2,4},{1,2,4},{2,3,4},{2,3,4} tiles the 4-cube, but the stored a(4) is 0.
- For n = 6 the output is exactly the two sets in the OEIS example.
- The number of strict tilings counted as placements (60, 168, 576, 1080, 2124, 3312, 5280, 7440, 10620, 14040 for n = 4..13) equals the value predicted by Theorem 2's parametrisation, after removing the double count when both slabs are cut at the same s.
- Set by set, the brute-force sets equal the Sigma(t,s,s') sets for n = 5..11.

(2) Method valid for all n: compress any tiling by 4 boxes to its reduced combinatorial type. Each axis has at most 8 endpoints, so each grid side is at most 7. I enumerated all tilings of all grids up to 7x7x7 by 4 boxes: 631,806 tilings, giving 102 reduced types, all with P+Q+R <= 6. typecount.c then runs every strictly increasing coordinate map for each type and n:
- strict counts for n = 1..200 equal (n-4)T(ceil((n-4)/2)) with 0 mismatches (21 types can give strict tiles);
- non-strict counts for n = 1..60 equal the A384311 b-file with 0 mismatches.

(3) Guillotine lemma: in every tiling of every grid up to 7^3 by 4 boxes, up to 5^3 by 3, and up to 3^3 by 2, I found 0 non-guillotine tilings. By the compression argument this check covers every combinatorial type, so it is an independent computer proof of Theorem 1 for k <= 4, real positions included. For k = 5, 2x2x2 already has 8 non-guillotine tilings out of 50. Restricting to P <= Q <= R reproduces the colleague's totals exactly: 420, 5040, 66920, and 876/41128.

(4) Other checks:
- The cube graph Q3 has 9 perfect matchings: 3 with all edges parallel and 6 of the claimed type II.
- My count of volume-matching candidate 4-sets reproduces their "cands" list for n = 1..20.
- For n <= 3000 the closed form, the m-form, the Berselli-type formula, the g.f. (via (1+x)^3(1-x)^4 * A(x) = x^5(1+x+4x^2)) and the order-7 recurrence for n >= 8 all agree. The recurrence fails at n = 7 if a(0) = 0, so "n >= 8" is correct.
- All 49 stored A386884 terms, all 45 stored A178312 terms and the 1001-term A178312 b-file match.

No disagreement anywhere.
gaps: No mathematical gap found. Each step checks out.

Minor, Remark 1.4: it explains the failure at k = 5 only by 'a tile may contain no corner at all' (the pinwheel's centre). The 2x2x2 example the remark cites fails differently: three 1x1x2 bars and two unit cubes, where every tile contains a corner and the unit cubes contain only one. The real point is that 8 <= 2k no longer forces each tile to hold exactly 2 corners. This only affects the explanation; the sharpness claim is true.

Minor, Section 6 item 3: guillotine_check.c covers only boxes with P <= Q <= R (that is where 420/5040/66920 and 41128/876 come from). This is complete up to symmetry, but the text says 'every box'. Also, sides <= 6 is not exhaustive for combinatorial types on its face; that would need sides up to 7. My run up to 7 shows every reduced 4-box type has extent at most 4, so their check happens to be complete. It is not used in the proof.

Cosmetic: for n = 1..3 the formula uses T at negative arguments (T(-1) = 0 with T(j) = j(j+1)/2). The proof says so explicitly, and A386884(n) = A178312(n-4) is claimed only for n >= 4, which is correct.
verify.details:
Definitions and offsets: A386884 has offset 1 and A178312 has offset 0, so A386884(n) = A178312(n-4) works for n >= 4 (A386884(5) = A178312(1) = 1). The reading "sets of 4 pairwise noncongruent strict shapes with integer sides that tile [0,n]^3" is forced by the data. It matches the a(6) example, all 49 stored terms (my brute force for n <= 13 plus the type method to n = 200), and, without strictness, A384311 to n = 60. The multiset reading is ruled out because it would make a(4) nonzero.

Proof check, step by step:
- Lemma 1.1 (cutting along a guillotine plane) holds.
- Lemma 1.2(a): a corner lies in a unique tile, via the delta-cube argument. (b): two corners differing in at least 2 coordinates, or 3 corners, force a tile to be full in two directions. (c): such a tile gives a guillotine plane at x_3 = d, using y - eps*e_3 in int P. All correct.
- Theorem 1: if no tile is full in two directions, each tile has at most 2 corners. Since 8 <= 2k, we get k = 4 with exactly 2 corners per tile, and these form a perfect matching of Q3. The parity count in Lemma 2.1 is correct, and the 9-matching classification checks by computer.
- Case I: the edge-covering argument gives a_1+a_2 = L_1 and the analogous relations. I re-derived the volume identity: it reduces to L_1L_2 + (a_1-a_4)(b_1-b_2). Both branches give a guillotine plane.
- Case II: the three vertical edges force h_1 = h_2 = L_3 - g_1 = L_3 - g_2.
- Theorem 2: the slabs are not strict, so the split is 2+2. Each slab splits by a k = 2 guillotine cut, and the cut cannot be along the thin axis, since that tile would be n x n x s. Strictness then gives s, s' not in {t, n-t}. The converse construction is right.
- Lemma 4.1: every edge has exactly one endpoint in O(t), so the distinctness criterion is right.
- Lemma 4.2: type A gives 4 vertices and C(m,2) sets. Type B gives 6 vertices, with O_0 recovered as the two degree-2 vertices and phi from their neighbourhoods, so m(m-1)(m-2) sets. Type C gives 5 vertices and C(m,2) sets. Different vertex counts make the types disjoint.
- Theorem 3: the algebra is right for both parities and for m = 0, 1.
- Appendix A (tilted tiles are impossible): steps (1) to (5) are valid. A non-axis-parallel tile at its f-minimal vertex has its tangent cone inside {w.x > 0}. The non-axis-parallel cones fill a union of orthants, which must be the single orthant O_{sigma*}. A measure count leaves one tile, and the extreme rays force it to be axis-parallel.
- Appendix B (integer positions) and the completeness of first-empty-cell backtracking are both correct.
- The consequences hold: g.f., Berselli-type formula (vanishing at n = 1..4), and the recurrence for n >= 8.

Independent confirmation goes beyond the hand proof: compressing to reduced types turns both the guillotine lemma (k <= 4) and the count for every n into finite checks. I ran those exhaustively, and the type count agrees with the formula for all n <= 200. Only cosmetic or wording issues remain.

Files are in /tmp/claude-0/deep/cuboids/verify1/:
- tile.c: tiling enumerator
- typecount.c: count from reduced types
- types4.txt: the 102 reduced types
- strict_types_1_200.txt: strict counts
- nonstrict2_1_60.txt: non-strict counts
- direct_11_13.txt: direct strict counts for n = 11..13
- formcheck.py: closed-form, g.f., recurrence and stored-data checks

novelty.prior_art:
I found no source stating A386884(n) = A178312(n-4), the closed form (n-4)T(ceil((n-4)/2)), the g.f., or the recurrence for A386884. A386884 (latest revision #16, Sep 28 2025) has no FORMULA lines, and its only cross-references are "Column 4 of A386903" and "Cf. A384311". A178312 has no geometric interpretation and no link to A386884. No sequence cross-references both, and the history and drafts show no one has proposed the match.

Partial prior art for supporting lemma (1) only:
- The OEIS A392884 comment by Diego Lago Gómez (Jul 04 2026) states it: "Conversely, every dissection of a box into at most 4 boxes has a fault plane (a plane meeting the interior of the box crossed by no piece); applying this recursively, I >= n^2 + n + 1." (https://oeis.org/A392884). It is given there without proof.
- The companion paper, D. Lago Gómez, "The minimum surface area of k unequal boxes tiling a cube: sharp thresholds, a fault-free law, and a reduction to two dimensions", arXiv:2607.15894 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15894), states and uses only the 2D version (Prop. 17 proof): "Every tiling by at most four rectangles has a fault line (the smallest non-guillotine tiling is the five-piece pinwheel)". Its Lemma 6 is the observation that a piece full in two directions gives a fault plane. That paper is about minimum surface area, not counting, and has nothing about strict cuboids, A386884 or A178312.

I found nothing on the slab structure theorem (2), the involution/graph-type count (4-cycles, two cherries, stars), or the rotated-box appendix (3).
novelty.details:
The target identity A386884(n) = (n-4)*T(ceil((n-4)/2)) = A178312(n-4) holds against all 49 terms in the OEIS data (n = 1..49). I found it stated nowhere: not in A386884 (Janaka Rodrigo, Aug 2025, terms by Sean A. Irvine, no formula), not in A178312 (Gary W. Adamson, 2010, pure arithmetic), not in A386903 (the parent array), and not in any other OEIS entry, arXiv paper or web page. The OEIS search on the distinctive run 1,2,9,12,30,36,70,... returns exactly these two sequences and no linking comment.

The one related prior statement is supporting lemma (1), that any box tiling by at most 4 boxes has a fault (guillotine) plane. Diego Lago Gómez asserts it, without proof, in a July 2026 comment in A392884 (minimum surface area of four distinct cuboids tiling the cube). His arXiv:2607.15894 proves related fault-plane facts (Lemma 6: a piece spanning two full directions gives a fault plane) and quotes the 2D pinwheel fact, but it does not count tilings and says nothing about strict shapes. The lemma alone does not make the counting identity immediate: the slab structure theorem and the three-type count (C(m,2) + m(m-1)(m-2) + [n even]C(m,2)) are still needed, and I found no prior version of either.

Verdict: NEW. If the identity goes into OEIS, A392884 / arXiv:2607.15894 should be cited as prior statements of the ≤4-box fault-plane lemma.

prove.theorem:
Let a(n)=A225034(n), offset 0: the number of binary words with exactly n 1's and at most n 0's that have no factor 101. Let D(n)=A005773(n), offset 0, with D(0)=1 and D(n) the number of directed animals of size n. Let b(n)=A048775(n), offset 1. Let c(n)=A163765(n), offset 1, defined by c(m+1)=Sum_{k=0..m}(-1)^(m-k)C(m,k)b(k+1). Let R(x) be the power series with constant term 1 and R^2=(1+x)/(1-3x). Then:
(1) For n>=1, a(n)=Sum_{k=0..n-1}(-1)^(n-1-k)C(n-1,k)C(2k+3,k+1). In words, (a(n+1))_{n>=0} is the inverse binomial transform of C(2n+3,n+1). Also a(n)=Sum_{j=0..n-1}C(n-1,j)C(j+3,n-j) and a(n)=[y^n](1-y+y^2)^(n-1)/(1-y)^(n+2).
(2) 2x*A(x)=(1+x)(R(x)-1), so A(x)=(1+x)(sqrt((1+x)/(1-3x))-1)/(2x). This equals the g.f. labeled 'Theorem' in A225034.
(3) a(0)=D(1)=1, and a(n)=D(n)+D(n+1) for all n>=1. This part uses the classical directed-animal g.f. Sum_{n>=1} D(n)x^n=(R-1)/2.
(4) A048775(n)=C(2n+1,n+1)-(n+1). Hence c(n)=a(n)-2[n=1]-[n=2]: c(1)=1, c(2)=6, and A163765(n)=A225034(n) for all n>=3.
(5) (n+1)a(n)-(2n+3)a(n-1)-3(n-2)a(n-2)=0 for all n>=2, and 2a(1)-5a(0)=1. This is Berselli's conjectured recurrence.
prove.proof_summary:
Write a word with n ones as 0^{g0} 1 0^{g1} 1 ... 1 0^{gn}. The word contains 101 exactly when some internal gap g_i (1<=i<=n-1) equals 1. Summing over at most n zeros gives a(n)=[y^n](1-y+y^2)^(n-1)(1-y)^-(n+2).
Expanding (1-y(1-y))^(n-1) by the binomial theorem gives the inverse-binomial-transform formula directly. A formal inverse-binomial-transform lemma (substitute x/(1+x)) combined with Sum C(2j,j)x^j=(1-4x)^(-1/2) then gives 2xA=(1+x)(R-1), where R=sqrt((1+x)/(1-3x)).
Algebraic simplification shows this equals the entry's 'Theorem' g.f. Comparing with the directed-animal g.f. (R-1)/2 gives a(n)=D(n)+D(n+1).
For A163765: the hockey-stick identity proves A048775(n)=C(2n+1,n+1)-(n+1). The inverse binomial transform of the correction term -(k+2) is -2[m=0]-[m=1], which gives A163765=A225034 for n>=3.
Finally, R satisfies (1+x)(1-3x)R'=2R. This turns 2xA=(1+x)(R-1) into the ODE x(1+x)(1-3x)A'+(1-5x)A=1+x. Reading off the coefficients gives Berselli's recurrence for n>=2.
prove.computations:
Everything below uses exact integer arithmetic. No mismatches were found anywhere.
- Brute-force enumeration of A225034 from its definition (enum101.c): n<=17.
- An independent 3-state automaton DP over (#1,#0) (verify.py): n<=1200. It agrees with the enumeration and with all 1001 b-file terms of A225034 (n<=1000).
- Lemma 1 coefficient formula checked for n<=60. The inverse-binomial formula checked for n<=1200. The positive double-sum formula checked for n<=300.
- a(n)=D(n)+D(n+1) checked for n<=1200, with D taken from an exact series square root. D was compared with all 201 b-file terms of A005773 (n<=200) and with brute-force directed animals (animals.py, n<=15, up to 1201917).
- Berselli's recurrence checked for 2<=n<=1200, in Python and in PARI (check_gf.gp).
- The entry's 'Theorem' g.f. and (1+x)(R-1)/(2x) both expand to the DP values: PARI n<=1200, sympy n<60.
- A048775: brute force of its definition for n<=9, the Sloane sum for n<=1201, and all 1000 b-file terms.
- A163765, computed from its definition, equals a(n)-2[n=1]-[n=2] for n<=1200 and matches all 28 stored terms.
- Arndt's comment, with 'length n', checked for n<=11 (arndt_check.py); 'length n+1' gives different numbers.
prove.whats_new:
A225034:
- Berselli's formula '(n+1)a(n)-(2n+3)a(n-1)-3(n-2)a(n-2)=0 for n>1' is labeled 'Conjecture'. It is now proved. It is in fact a formal consequence of the g.f. the entry already labels 'Theorem' (Bilotta-Grazzini-Pergola 2013, Prop. 4 with j=1, proved by the ECO method), because that g.f. simplifies to (1+x)(R-1)/(2x), which satisfies the first-order ODE above. The label can be removed.
- That 'Theorem' g.f. now also has an independent, elementary proof from the definition.
- New formulas, none of them in the entry: a(n)=A005773(n)+A005773(n+1) for n>=1; a(n)=Sum_{k=0..n-1}(-1)^(n-1-k)C(n-1,k)C(2k+3,k+1); a(n)=Sum_j C(n-1,j)C(j+3,n-j); a(n)=[y^n](1-y+y^2)^(n-1)/(1-y)^(n+2); the simplified g.f. (1+x)(sqrt((1+x)/(1-3x))-1)/(2x); and a(n)=A163765(n) for n>=3.
- Missing cross-references: A005773, A163765, A048775, A001700.
- Side finding: Arndt's comment says 'length n+1', but the correct statement is length n with n+2 letters. The words in its own example have length n, and length n+1 gives A025565(n+2) instead. The corrected statement is proved in Section 7 of the proof.

A163765:
- The entry has only its definition and a cross-reference to A048775. New: A163765(n)=A225034(n)=A005773(n)+A005773(n+1) for n>=3, with A163765(1)=1 and A163765(2)=6. Its g.f. is A(x)-1-2x-x^2. For n>=3 it therefore counts 101-avoiding words. It satisfies Berselli's recurrence for n>=5.

A005773:
- It could get the cross-reference A005773(n)+A005773(n+1)=A225034(n) for n>=1.

Dependency: the A005773 link uses only the classical directed-animal g.f. (Dhar 1982; Gouyou-Beauchamps-Viennot 1988).

Scripts in /tmp/claude-0/deep/words101/: enum101.c, verify.py (log in verify.log), check_gf.gp, animals.py, arndt_check.py.

verify.independent_computation:
I wrote my own code in /tmp/claude-0/deep/words101/verify1/ and only looked at the colleague's files to read the BGP paper text. I downloaded fresh b-files from oeis.org.
(i) bf.c is a pure brute force from the definition. It enumerates every bit string of length L<=34, counts the ones and zeros, and detects the factor 101 with x&~(x>>1)&(x>>2) under a length mask. It gives A225034(0..17) = 1,3,7,18,...,39809649, which matches the OEIS data.
(ii) dp.py is my own 3-state suffix automaton DP over (#1,#0), run to n=1300. It agrees with the brute force for n<=17 and with all 1001 b-file terms (n<=1000).
(iii) checks.py: the inverse-binomial formula Sum(-1)^(n-1-k)C(n-1,k)C(2k+3,k+1) and the positive sum Sum C(n-1,j)C(j+3,n-j) both equal a(n) for 1<=n<=1300.
(iv) animals_own.py is my own brute-force generator of directed site animals, grown by adding N/E successor cells and deduplicated as frozensets. For sizes 1..14 it gives 1,2,5,...,414584 = A005773. checks2.py computes D from the exact integer series square root (1+R)/2. That D matches all A005773 b-file terms (n<=200) and Somos' recurrence. a(0)=D(1), and a(n)=D(n)+D(n+1) holds for 1<=n<=1300, while D(0)+D(1)=2 is not a(0).
(v) 2xA=(1+x)(R-1) holds coefficientwise to x^1301. Berselli's recurrence holds for 2<=n<=1300, and 2a(1)-5a(0)=1.
(vi) A048775 brute force of the definition (intervals times nondecreasing maps) for n<=7 gives 1,7,31,121,456,1709,6427. The b-file equals C(2n+1,n+1)-(n+1) for n<=1000.
(vii) A163765 built from its definition, c(m+1)=Sum(-1)^(m-k)C(m,k)b(k+1), reproduces all 28 stored terms and the entry's example 48=(-1,3,-3,1).(1,7,31,121). It equals a(n)-2[n=1]-[n=2] for n<=1300, and also for n<=1000 when the raw A048775 b-file values are used instead of the formula.
(viii) PARI (g.gp): the entry's 'Theorem' g.f. and (1+x)(sqrt((1+x)/(1-3x))-1)/(2x) both expand to the DP values to O(x^1300). The coefficient form [y^n](1-y+y^2)^(n-1)/(1-y)^(n+2) is right for 1<=n<=250, and in fact also at n=0. The ODE x(1+x)(1-3x)A'+(1-5x)A=1+x has zero residual.
(ix) lemma1.py: Lemma 1's bivariate W(n,m)=[y^m](1-y)^-2(1/(1-y)-y)^(n-1) matches my DP for all n,m<=40. sympy confirms Lemma 6, the ODE, G=A and identity (4.1).
(x) Arndt's comment: weakly increasing words of length n over n+2 letters with no up-step of 1 give 1,3,7,18,48,... = a(n) for n<=10. Length n+1 gives 2,4,10,26,70,192,... instead.
There were no disagreements anywhere.
gaps: Not an error, but a dependency: Part 3, a(n)=D(n)+D(n+1), is proved only from the external classical theorem that directed animals on the square lattice have g.f. (R-1)/2 (Dhar 1982; Gouyou-Beauchamps-Viennot 1988; Bousquet-Melou 1998). The proof states this openly. My brute force of animals up to size 14 and the b-file comparison support it, but this part is only as proved as that cited theorem.

Wording only: the target title 'A225034 = inverse binomial transform of A048775' is false at n=1,2 (c(1)=1 vs a(1)=3, c(2)=6 vs a(2)=7). The precise claim c(n)=a(n)-2[n=1]-[n=2], with equality for n>=3, is correct and proved.

Minor and harmless: (2.1) is stated for n>=1 with a(0)=1 handled separately, but the coefficient formula also holds at n=0. The remark that c satisfies Berselli's recurrence for n>=5 is correct and sharp: the left side is 15 at n=3 and 6 at n=4.
verify.details:
I checked every step against the OEIS entries (snapshot and live are the same: A225034 #75, A163765 #7) and found no error.

Definitions and offsets: A225034 has offset 0 and counts factor (not subsequence) avoidance, which the n=2 example confirms because it lists 1001. A005773 has offset 0 with D(0)=1, and its listed g.f. 1/2+(1/2)sqrt((1+x)/(1-3x)) gives Sum_{n>=1}D(n)x^n=(R-1)/2. A048775 has offset 1. A163765 has offset 1, and the definition 'inverse binomial transform assuming offset zero in both' read as (0.1) reproduces the data and the example. All match exactly.

Lemma 1: the gap bijection is correct. A factor 101 forces two consecutive ones with exactly one zero between them, so it occurs iff some internal gap g_i equals 1. The internal-gap factor 1/(1-y)-y, the end-gap factors, and the partial-sum factor 1/(1-y) are all right.

Lemma 2 and Corollary 2': the expansions 1-y+y^2 = 1-y(1-y) = (1-y)^2+y, the index changes (r=n+2-k>=3, j=n-k>=1; i=n-1-k) and the upper-negation step leading to C(j+3,n-j) are all correct.

Lemma 3: the inverse binomial transform g.f. S(x/(1+x))/(1+x) is standard, and the proof is formally valid.

Lemma 4: 1-4z = (1-3x)/(1+x), C(2N,N) = 2C(2N-1,N-1), and the series-root uniqueness argument are all fine.

Part 2: the algebra 2x^2T = (1+x)(R-1)-2x leading to 2xA = (1+x)(R-1) is correct. The factorization Delta = (1-x)^2(1+x)(1-3x), Q = (1-x)(1-3x)R, and the identity (1+x)(R-1)(1-3x)(1+R) = 4x(1+x) are correct, so the g.f. equals the entry's 'Theorem' g.f. The BGP paper's Proposition 4 with j=1 is exactly that g.f.

Part 4: Lemma 5 follows from the double hockey-stick (r=n-1>=0, then r=n). E(m) = 2[m=0]+[m=1], which gives c(1)=1, c(2)=6 and c(n)=a(n) for n>=3.

Part 5: Lemma 6, (1+x)(1-3x)R' = 2R, is correct, and the ODE x(1+x)(1-3x)A'+(1-5x)A = 1+x is derived correctly (I re-derived it by hand and checked it with sympy). Extracting [x^n] gives (n+1)a(n)-(2n+3)a(n-1)-3(n-2)a(n-2) = [n=0]+[n=1], which is Berselli's recurrence for n>1.

The Section 7 correction to Arndt's comment ('length n', not 'length n+1') is correct and its proof is valid.

No finite case is left open by any argument. The computations only confirm results that are proved for all n. My independent code is in /tmp/claude-0/deep/words101/verify1/: bf.c, dp.py, checks.py, checks2.py, animals_own.py, g.gp, lemma1.py and arndt.py.

novelty.prior_art:
(a) The generating function (part 2) is known. A225034 itself has "%F Theorem: G.f. = 2*(1-x^2)/(3*x^2-4*x+1+sqrt((1-x^2)^2-4*(x-x^2)*(1-x^2)))", from Bilotta–Grazzini–Pergola, JIS 16 (2013), Prop. 4 with j=1 (https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL16/Grazzini/grazzini2.html). Merlini–Nocentini, JIS 21 (2018) Art. 18.1.3 (https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL21/Merlini/merlini5.html), Sec. 3.1, give "S^[101](t) = (1+t)(1-3t-sqrt(1-2t-3t^2))/(2t(3t-1))". Since sqrt(1-2t-3t^2)/(1-3t)=R, this is literally (1+t)(R-1)/(2t). They add: "As pointed out by an anonymous referee, the previous functions can be rewritten as S^[101](t) = (1+t)(1-tM(t))/(1-3t) ... S^[101](t) = (1+t)M(t)/(1-tM(t)) = (1+tM(t))^2/(1-tM(t))", and say identity (3) "has a combinatorial interpretation in terms of compact-rooted directed animals". The OEIS also has it: A225034 says "Row sums of the Riordan array in A239101", and A239101 says "Riordan array (f(x), (f(x)-1)/(2*f(x))) where f(x) = sqrt((1+x)/(1-3*x))" (Deléham 2014). The row-sum g.f. 2f^2/(f+1) simplifies at once to (1+x)(f-1)/(2x).
(b) Part 3 (a(n)=A005773(n)+A005773(n+1)) is not stated anywhere I found. It is immediate from Merlini–Nocentini's (1+t)M/(1-tM) together with the A005773 formula "G.f.: 1/(1-x*G(x)) where G(x) is g.f. of A001006", because M/(1-tM)=(D-1)/t.
(c) Part 1 is not stated explicitly, but two existing formulas give it in a line or two. A005773 has Barry's "a(n+1) = Sum_{k=0..n} (-1)^(n+k)*C(n,k)*C(2*k+1,k+1)"; adding consecutive terms and using Pascal's rule gives (1). A180562's "T(n,k) = Sum_j (-1)^j C(n-k-1,j) C(|n-2j|,k-j)", summed with the hockey stick, also gives (1). The form Sum C(n-1,j)C(j+3,n-j) follows from Arndt's A225034 comment (n-multisets of n+2 letters with no up-step 1). Baril–Bevan–Kirgizov's Table 1 (n-multisets of [k] with no consecutive integers) contains A225034 as its k=n+2 diagonal (3,7,18,48,...), though they do not say so.
(d) Part 4: A048775 already states "a(n) = binomial(2*n+1, n+1)-(n+1)", and A048775 says it "Equals binomial transform of A163765". No OEIS entry, paper or web page links A163765 to A225034. Neither entry cross-references the other, and the two term runs appear only in these two entries.
(e) Part 5: A225034 still carries "Conjecture: (n+1)*a(n) - (2*n+3)*a(n-1) - 3*(n-2)*a(n-2) = 0 for n>1. - Bruno Berselli, May 02 2013", in both the snapshot and online. I found no published proof, including in Sela Fried's four OEIS-conjecture papers. It follows routinely from the known algebraic g.f.
(f) Not relevant to the identities: Archer–Graves (arXiv:2205.09686, Fig. 2 and Thm 4.2) identify 2*A225034 with Dyck paths having L(D)=5, g.f. 2x^5(1+xm)^3(x^2(xm)'+1).
novelty.details:
All five claims check out numerically for n<20, including brute-force counting of 101-avoiding words for n<=7, A163765(n)=A225034(n) for n=3..20 with c(1)=1, c(2)=6, Berselli's recurrence for n>=2, and 2a(1)-5a(0)=1.

What is known: the core object, the algebraic g.f. A(x)=(1+x)(R-1)/(2x), is established. It appears as the 'Theorem' g.f. (Bilotta–Grazzini–Pergola 2013), in Merlini–Nocentini 2018 in a form that is literally (1+t)(R-1)/(2t), and as the row sums of the Riordan array A239101 (f,(f-1)/(2f)) with f=R. Merlini–Nocentini also give S^[101]=(1+t)M/(1-tM). Combined with A005773's g.f. 1/(1-xM), that makes a(n)=D(n)+D(n+1) immediate, though nobody writes it down. Formula (1) follows within a line or two from Barry's formula in A005773, or from the explicit formula in A180562. Part (4)'s closed form for A048775 is stated in A048775.

What is not recorded anywhere I found: (i) the coincidence A163765(n)=A225034(n) for n>=3 (neither entry references the other and no paper mentions both); (ii) the explicit inverse-binomial-transform formula, the identity a(n)=A005773(n)+A005773(n+1), and the 'directed animals' link for A225034 itself; (iii) a written proof of Berselli's 2013 recurrence, which OEIS still labels a conjecture, although it follows routinely from the known algebraic g.f. via the ODE x(1+x)(1-3x)A'+(1-5x)A=1+x.

So the new parts are the A163765/A225034 identification, the explicit statement of (1) and (3), and a written proof that settles the conjecture. They are short derivations from known g.f.s and formulas, not independent discoveries, hence PARTIALLY_KNOWN rather than NEW. Downloaded texts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-test1/92b0ad82-0425-5b2b-85ed-b7d12d7491b1/scratchpad/ (bgp.txt, mn.txt, ag.txt, bbk.txt); the verification script is chk.py there.

prove.theorem:
Definition. Take a 0/1 array x with rows 0..n and columns 0..k. For each 2x2 block set D(i,j) = x(i,j) + x(i+1,j+1) - x(i,j+1) - x(i+1,j), for 0 <= i <= n-1 and 0 <= j <= k-1. The array is valid when, wherever both entries exist:
- (V1) D(i,j) <= D(i,j+1);
- (V2) D(i,j) <= D(i+1,j);
- (V3) D(i,j+1) <= D(i+1,j) (nondecreasing going from NE to SW).

T(n,k), for n,k >= 1, is the number of valid (n+1)x(k+1) arrays. A253435 lists it by antidiagonals with offset 1: a(1)=T(1,1), then T(1,2), T(2,1), and so on. This reading was confirmed against the data. The opposite V3 direction gives the transposed table, and the other diagonal gives T(2,2)=72 instead of 58.

Theorem. For all n,k >= 1:
- T(n,k) = 9*2^(n-1) + 9*2^(k-1) + 12 for n >= 2 and k >= 4 (so in particular for all n,k >= 4).
- T(1,k) = T(k,1) = 9*2^(k-1) + 37 for k >= 4.
- T(n,2) = 9*2^(n-1) + 36 for n >= 4.
- T(n,3) = 9*2^(n-1) + 49 for n >= 3.
- For n,k <= 3 the rows are (16,39,69), (39,58,70), (69,73,85).

Classification, for n >= 3, k >= 2, max(n,k) >= 4. Valid arrays are exactly:
- Row type (9*2^(n-1) arrays): rows R_1..R_{n-1} are constant rows, R_0 is in {0^,1^,01^k}, and R_n is in {0^,1^,0^k1}.
- Frozen type (S_k arrays): R_1 = ... = R_{n-1} = W with W non-constant, and R_0, R_n are bounded-defect completions of W. Here S_2 = 36, S_3 = 49, and S_k = 9*2^(k-1) + 12 for k >= 4.
prove.proof_summary:
1. Rectangle sums. Any rectangle sum of D telescopes to x(a,c) - x(a,d) - x(b,c) + x(b,d), so it lies in [-2,2]. Together with monotonicity, positive D entries can only be in the last two rows and last two columns, and negative entries only in the first two rows and columns.

2. Lemma 1. Short 2x2 rectangle arguments, which use V3 and need max(n,k) >= 4, cut this down further. Negative entries can only be at (0,0) and (0,1); positive entries only at (n-1,k-2) and (n-1,k-1).

3. Proposition 2 (exact characterization). An array is valid exactly when D is zero outside those four cells and D(0,0) <= D(0,1) <= 0 <= D(n-1,k-2) <= D(n-1,k-1).

4. Row decomposition. In terms of row differences d_i = R_{i+1} - R_i:
- every middle d_i is a constant vector, so the middle rows are either all one non-constant row W, or each is a constant row (2^(n-1) choices);
- d_0 must be one of 7 explicit "TL patterns";
- d_{n-1} must be the mirror image of one.
Counting completions gives f(constant row) = 3 and g = f composed with complement-reversal, with explicit tables. So T(n,k) = 2^(n-3)*6*6 + S_k = 9*2^(n-1) + S_k.

5. Lemma 6. S_k = 9*2^(k-1) + 12 for k >= 4. The sum of (1+w0)(2-w_k) over all words is 9*2^(k-1), and a fixed set of 14 exceptional words adds a correction of +12.

6. Remaining rows and columns. n = 2, n = 1 and k = 1 (by transposition) are handled the same way. The 3x3 corner is checked by exhaustive enumeration.
prove.computations:
Independent implementations, all in /tmp/claude-0/deep/hardin-table/:
- brute.c: exhaustive enumeration of every size with (n+1)(k+1) <= 26 (40 entries). It also tests the alternative readings of the definition.
- check_char.c: exhaustive check of Lemma 1 and Proposition 2 on 23 sizes. All 21 sizes satisfying the hypothesis show 0 mismatches. (4,1) is a control outside the hypothesis that reports mismatches as expected, and (3,3) also matches.
- check_fg.py: brute-force check of the 7 TL patterns, the f and g tables, g = f composed with complement-reversal, S_k for 2 <= k <= 10, F = G = 6, the 14-word table of Lemma 6 for k = 4..9, and the n = 1 count.
- dp.cpp: transfer matrix over pairs of rows with pruned DFS. Widths 2..24 were run in both orientations: up to 60 rows for widths <= 22, and 30 rows for widths 23-24 (37.7M states).
- dp_big.py: independent big-integer transfer matrix for widths 2..8, up to 210 rows.

Results:
- compare_all.py: 4211 distinct (n,k), covering every entry with min(n,k) <= 23 (other side up to 30, 60 or 210). 1047 entries were computed twice independently. There are 0 mismatches with the theorem.
- All 1101 b-file terms of A253435 (every entry with n+k <= 47) were independently recomputed and agree.
- All 210-term b-files of A253152, A253429-A253434 and A253436-A253441 agree with the theorem, as does the 26-term b-file of A253428.
- check_gf.py: every empirical formula in these entries was checked to 400 terms (closed forms, recurrences, and Barker g.f.s to 60 coefficients). All hold, and every stated threshold is sharp.

verify.independent_computation:
I wrote all my code from the OEIS wording and did not reuse theirs. It is in /tmp/claude-0/deep/hardin-table/verify1/.

(1) bf.c is an exhaustive brute force over all (n+1)x(k+1) 0/1 arrays. It tests five readings of the third condition: NE<=SW, SW<=NE, NW<=SE, SE<=NW, and none. It covers all 40 sizes with (n+1)(k+1) <= 26.
- The NE<=SW reading (D(i,j+1) <= D(i+1,j)) reproduces every OEIS term in range, including the asymmetric pairs T(2,3)=70 / T(3,2)=73, T(2,4)=102 / T(4,2)=108 and T(3,4)=120 / T(4,3)=121.
- The SW<=NE reading gives exactly the transposed table.
- The NW<=SE reading gives T(2,2)=72. It is in fact implied by V1+V2, so it equals the count without a third condition.

(2) tm.cpp is a transfer matrix that builds the array row by row. Its state is the last two rows, and each next row is found by a column-wise search with the row, vertical and NE-SW checks.
- Mode 0 gives T(n, w-1). Mode 1 uses the mirrored rule and gives T(w-1, n), which serves as a second, transposed computation.
- Counts use exact 128-bit integers.
- The one pruning rule (a rectangle-sum bound) was shown to change nothing: pruned and unpruned versions agree for widths 2..12.
- Widths 2..18 were run to 120 rows and widths 19..22 to 70 rows, in both modes.
- Result: 4199 distinct (n,k), including every entry with min(n,k) <= 21 and max <= 70, and every entry with min <= 17 and max <= 120. 441 entries were computed in both orientations and agree. All 40 brute-force entries agree.
- There are 0 mismatches with the claimed closed form.

(3) I downloaded the b-files from oeis.org myself:
- A253435: all 1101 terms (every entry with n+k <= 47, plus part of n+k = 48) agree with the theorem. 1091 of them were also computed by my transfer matrix.
- A253152, A253429-A253434 and A253436-A253441 (210 terms each) and A253428 (26 terms): all agree.
- Barker's g.f.s for the 11 column/row entries with one (A253152, A253429-A253431, A253433-A253434, A253436-A253438, A253440-A253441) match the theorem for 40 coefficients each.

(4) lem.c checks the lemmas exhaustively, over all arrays. On 25 sizes satisfying (H), including (1,4..12), (2,4..7), (3,4..6), (4,2..5), (5,2..4), (6,2..3), (7,2) and (8,2), I found 0 violations of (F2), of Lemma 1, or of Proposition 2 in either direction. The classification also holds on the 16 of those sizes with n >= 2: row-type count = 9*2^(n-1), frozen count = S_k, no other arrays. At (3,3) the equivalence also holds; outside (H) at (2,2), (2,3), (3,2), (1,2) and (1,3) it fails, as expected.

(5) lem46.py and k3.py check the counting lemmas by brute force over all R:
- Lemma 3: exactly 7 TL triples.
- Lemma 4 (f and g, including g(W) = f(W~)): 0 mismatches for every W with 2 <= k <= 12.
- S_k equals 36, 49 and 9*2^(k-1)+12 for k = 2..12.
- Every entry of the k=3 table of 14 words matches.
- The n=1 weights by e are TL {-1:6, 0:6, 1:1} and BR {-1:6, 0:6, 1:1}.
gaps: No mathematical gap found. Every step was checked by hand and tested by brute force: (F1), (F2), Lemma 1 cases (b), (b'), (c), (c'), Proposition 2 in both directions, the 5.1 translation, Lemmas 3-6, cases (a)-(e) and the coverage argument.

Cosmetic: the task statement's 'bounded-defect completions' is undefined there. Proof.md defines the frozen-type completions precisely as W - d with d a TL pattern and W + d' with d' a BR pattern (Lemma 4).

Cosmetic: the direction of the third condition is fixed by matching the data, since the OEIS name is ambiguous. This is unavoidable, and I confirmed it independently: the NE<=SW reading matches all 40 brute-forced sizes, and my transfer matrix reproduces the 1091 b-file terms it reaches.

Cosmetic: the classification is stated only for n >= 3. The n = 2 count in case (b) uses the same split (18 + S_k), which my brute force confirms, but that split is not stated as part of the classification.
Wording only, not part of the proof: 'covering every entry with min(n,k) <= 23' in the computation summary is limited by the length run on the other side (30, 60 or 210).
verify.details:
How I checked the proof:
- (F1) telescopes correctly, so every rectangle sum of D lies in [-2,2].
- (F2) follows from the chains in V1/V2 together with that bound.
- Lemma 1 under (H):
  - Case (b) is correct. The chain D(0,0) <= D(0,1) <= D(1,1) and D(1,0) <= D(1,1) would make the 2x2 sum <= -4.
  - Case (c) correctly uses V3 at (0,0), which gives D(0,1) <= D(1,0), to force D(1,1) >= 1. Then (F2) gives n,k <= 3, contradicting max(n,k) >= 4.
  - Cases (b') and (c') are the symmetric arguments and are also correct.
  - For n = 1, (H) forces k >= 4, so C- and C+ are disjoint.
- Proposition 2, converse direction: every inequality D(a) <= D(b) with a in C+ or b in C- is either vacuous or part of (Ch). I checked this instance by instance.
- Section 5.1: D(i,j) = d_i(j+1) - d_i(j), and rows 0 and n-1 are distinct when n >= 2, so the TL, middle and BR conditions are independent.
- Lemma 3: correct, 7 patterns.
- Lemma 4: I rederived all 8 table entries of A_0 and A_1. The complement-reversal identity (W~ - R~)(j) = (R - W)(k-j) holds.
- Lemma 5: correct.
- Lemma 6:
  - For k >= 4, W' and V overlap at position 2, so |E| = 14. The four family tables are correct (sums 18+4+4+18 = 44 against baseline 10+4+4+10+4 = 32), giving S_k = 9*2^(k-1)+12.
  - The k=2 and k=3 tables are correct entry by entry.
- Cases (a)-(e):
  - (a) For m = n-1 >= 2, R_1 and R_{n-1} are distinct choices, giving 2^(n-3)*6*6 = 9*2^(n-1).
  - (b) For n = 2 the count is S_k + 18.
  - (c) For n = 1 the count is 36 + 36*2^(k-3) + 1 (TL and BR weights both 6, 6, 1 for e = -1, 0, 1).
  - (d) For k = 1, transposition preserves D and swaps V1 with V2, while V3 is vacuous.
  - (e) The 9 entries with n,k <= 3 are confirmed by my brute force.
  - Coverage of all (n,k) is complete, and T(3,3) = 85 = 36+49 justifies the n >= 3 threshold for k = 3.
- Offsets and indexing are correct: A253435 is read by antidiagonals with n increasing, the column/row entries have offset 1, A253431 = T(n,4) and A253438 = T(4,n).

My own computations found no discrepancy anywhere: brute force, a transfer matrix in both orientations, exhaustive lemma checks and the oeis.org b-files. The proof is complete and correct for all n,k >= 1.

- google-deepmind/formal-conjectures and epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems file lists
- Adamczewski, "OEIS Open", arXiv:2608.11941
- Tong Niu's short-proof papers, arXiv:2605.14213 and 2605.15500
- Google-style searches for the A-numbers on GitHub, MathOverflow and StackExchange, and for Monge-type 2x2 minor monotonicity counts.

Direct GitHub code and issue search was blocked by the session's GitHub policy, so it was not done.
novelty.prior_art:
Only conjectures (Hardin's "Empirical" formulas) were found. No proof exists anywhere I could reach.

1. A253435 itself (R. H. Hardin, Dec 31 2014, https://oeis.org/A253435) says: "Empirical: T(n,k) = 9*2(n-1) + 9*2^(k-1) + c, where rows n=1 c=28 for k>3; n>1 c=12 for k>3; columns k=1 c=28 for n>3; k=2 c=18 for n>3; k=3 c=13 for n>2; k>3 c=12 for n>1". The missing ^ is in the original. It also gives "Empirical for columns: k=1: 9*2^(n-1) + 37 for n>3; k=2: 9*2^(n-1) + 36 for n>3; k=3: 9*2^(n-1) + 49 for n>2; k=4: 9*2^(n-1) + 84 for n>1 ...", "Empirical for rows: n=1: 9*2^(k-1) + 37 for k>3; n=2: ... + 30; n=3: ... + 48; n=4: ... + 84 ...", and the full table of c including the 3x3 corner.

2. Sibling entries outside the pairs state the same formulas, all marked empirical:
   - A253428 (diagonal): "Empirical: a(n) = 9*2^n + 12 for n>3"
   - A253429: "Empirical: a(n) = 9*2^(n-1) + 36 for n>3"
   - A253430: "Empirical: a(n) = 9*2^(n-1) + 49 for n>2"
   - A253432: "+156 for n>1"
   - A253436: "+30 for k>3"
   - A253437: "+48 for n>3"
   - A253439: "+156 for n>3"
   - A253152 (row/column 1, from the companion table A253159): "Empirical: a(n) = 9*2^(n-1) + 37 for n>3"
   Colin Barker added "Empirical g.f." lines in 2018.

3. The pair entries A253431/A253438, A253433/A253440 and A253434/A253441 give the column formula "9*2^(n-1)+c for n>1" and the row formula "9*2^(n-1)+c for n>3" separately, again as empirical. None of them says the column and its paired row coincide.

4. Nearest proved relative: Sela Fried, "Proofs of several OEIS conjectures on determinants and permanents", arXiv:2606.09913, pp. 29-31 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09913). It proves Hardin's A250742, T(n,k) = 2^(n+1)+2^(k+1)-2, and A250742 now has the comment "These observations are true (see Fried link)". That table has a different, stronger condition, which forces every 2x2 difference D to be 0 and gives banded arrays. It does not cover the D-monotonicity conditions of A253435 or A253159.

5. Hardinian Arrays (arXiv:2309.00487) is about Hardin's king-move tables (A253026, A253223, A253004) and is unrelated. None of the other OEIS-proof papers or Lean datasets mention any A2531xx-A2534xx entry.
novelty.details:
The closed forms are Hardin's 2014 empirical conjectures, stated in A253435 and in all of its row, column and diagonal entries. Nobody has proved them. No OEIS entry, paper, arXiv preprint, formal-conjecture dataset or website I found gives a proof, the row-type/frozen-type classification, the rectangle-sum argument, or the resulting coincidences between paired rows and columns (A253431/A253438, A253433/A253440, A253434/A253441 agreeing for n >= 4). What is new is therefore the theorem with its proof and classification. The formulas themselves are not new: every value in the claimed theorem matches the conjectured c-table in A253435, including:
- c=12 for n>=2, k>=4
- 9*2^(k-1)+37 for row and column 1
- column 2: +36 for n>=4
- column 3: +49 for n>=3
- the 3x3 corner (16,39,69 / 39,58,70 / 69,73,85)

The OEIS validity ranges agree with the theorem's ranges, for example columns k>=4 "for n>1" and rows "for k>3". I also checked the claimed formula against all 1101 terms of b253435.txt (every n,k with n+k <= 48, read by antidiagonals T(1,1), T(1,2), T(2,1), ...). There were no mismatches.

One typo in A253435 for whoever writes this up: "9*2(n-1)" should read "9*2^(n-1)".

The closest proved result is Fried 2026 (arXiv:2606.09913) for Hardin's A250742. It uses the same "2x2 differences telescope" idea, but in a degenerate case where all D vanish, so it does not imply the A253435 result. The companion table A253159 (horizontal and vertical monotonicity only, whose row 1 is A253152 = T(1,k) here) is also unproved. Its empirical formula, T(n,k) = 9*2^(n-1)+9*2^(k-1)+c with c=28/30/21/20, could be a natural follow-up, since the same method seems likely to apply.

Caveat: arXiv API full-text search was rate-limited and GitHub code search was blocked. Coverage of GitHub-hosted AI-proof projects is therefore incomplete; for example, the-omega-institute/trureturing showed up in web search but could not be searched for these A-numbers.
